full_judgment:
M Moazzam Husain, J : This rule, at the instance of three accused-students, was taken challenging the legality of the proceedings in Special Tribunal Case No. 63 of 1996 under section 361A of the Cede of Criminal Procedure now pending for disposal, in the Special Tribunal No. 1 Comilla, awaiting charge to be framed. 

 2. Facts, in brief, are that a BDR patrol party while, coming back to its camp having finished routine patrol duty received information that three persons coming on a rickshaw towards Comilla town from the side of Golabari Hat. The moment the rickshaw came close to them they stopped it and put its passengers under interrogation. Under interrogation they plainly disclosed that they were Bangladeshi; they went to Agartala, India, just on a visit; from there they bought different trifling things of personal use and were returning home. When they disclosed, on query that they had no travel document they were arrested on the charge of going to India without valid travel documents. After arrest they were searched in presence of people gathering around. On search a) woolen sweater-2 pieces b) half sleeve ganjee-3 pieces c) pen, Taka 25 each, 4 pieces d) Indian Cine magazine-2 copies e) Novel wrist watch (used) 1 piece f) waist coat valued Taka 400/- 1 piece i) cigarette 1 packet j) Bangladesh currency notes of various denominations amounting of Taka 616.50 h) Cuban 10p coin 1 piece and k) music cassette 3 pieces. Total value of the goods seized from three accused as assessed was Taka 3,951.50, i.e., less than four thousand Taka were recovered from their possessions. The goods were deposited in the customs godown and the present case was lodged in the local police station surrendering the arrestees there as the accused persons by bringing in the aforesaid goods into Bangladesh have committed “অবৈধভাবে ভারতীয় মালামাল পাচারের অপরাধ (act of smuggling into Bangladesh foreign Foods punishable u/s 25B of the Special Powers Act, 1974). 

 3. One Sub-Inspector of police investigated into the case and having found prima facie truth in the allegation submitted charge-sheet u/s 25B of the Special Powers Act (SPA). Thereafter the case was sent up to the Court the Sessions and Special Tribunal, Comilla wherein it was registered as STC No. 63 of 1995. Cognizance of the offence was taken by the Tribunal No. 1 and a date for framing charge was accordingly fixed. Soon thereafter the present rule and stay were taken. Thus the case is still pending before the said Tribunal for disposal. 

 4. Contentions of the petitioners, in short, are that all of them are young boys and regular students of different colleges at Chittagong. They come of very respectable families having had no previous criminal records. On a vacation the trio came to Comilla just to visit places of interest like Mainamati and BARD. On the second day of the visit they went .to the border area out of curiosity. On the way they reached a Bazar called Bibir Bazar, a Bazar close to Indian border wherefrom they bought some trifling things of personal use and took their way back to Comilla on a rickshaw. Suddenly they were waylaid by some BDR members and subjected to interrogation. They made a plain disclosure of everything. Despite the fact they were arrested and all their belongings were taken away including the little of Bangladesh currency notes kept to meet the bus fare up to Chittagong. Their further contention is that they did not visit India and were well within the territory of Bangladesh. The trifling things of personal use are all available in border-area and sold in open market. The so called confessional statements allegedly made to the BDR personnel were extorted and were immediately retracted. The point most relevant for the case raised by the petitioners is that even if the allegation made is taken to be true does not constitute any offence at all under any law far less one under section 25B of the SPA in that a Bangladeshi tourist coming back with bare accompaniments of life, even if of foreign origin, does not constitute offence as contemplated u/s 25B of the Special Powers Act merely because he/she is not possessed of any travel document. The young boys have fallen victims to grudge of the members of the BDR who failed to realize illegal gratifications from them from the aforesaid factual background what is deduced is that the articles allegedly recovered from the possession of three boys are undeniably petty things of personal use which are nothing more than personal belongings which by no stretch of imagination be relatable to commercial consignment or huge issue like national economy. Nevertheless the case is going to decide no less a thing than the fate and career of three young boys who are none but three students having all their lives and career ahead. The fact begs the vexing question: can the act of bringing into Bangladesh small things irrespective of nature and kind such as things of day-to-day use as were recovered in the instant case, be called 'smuggling' as contemplated under section 25B of the SPA and destroy lives of a couple of otherwise bright students having unblemished past. Or in other words, did the legislature intend such absurd or irrational result by the applications of its enactment. Before embarking upon discussion on the question it would be apt to turn back to the law in order to ascertain the legislative intent behind enactment of such a stringent law especially when similar provisions dealing with prevention and punishment of smuggling in the Customs Act was in operation. 

 b) gold bullion, silver bullion, platinum, palladium, radium, precious stones, currency, manufactures of gold or silver or platinum of palladium, or precious stones or any other goods notified by the government in the official gazette, in each case exceeding Taka ten lac  in value; or 

 8. From the provisions of law quoted above it is clear that smuggling is still dwelling in its usual habitat, i.e., the Customs Act. In the Customs Act smuggling means to bring into or take out of Bangladesh, in breach of any prohibition or restriction for the time being in force, or evading payment of customs duties or taxes leviable thereon narcotics, drugs or psychotropic substance; or gold bullion, silver bullion. platinum, palladium, radium, precious stones, currency, manufactures of gold or silver or platinum of palladium or any other goods notified by the government in the official gazette (in each case exceeding Taka ten lac in value) or any goods concealed in any manner or any other goods by any route other than a route authorized by law from any place other than a customs station and includes an attempt, abetment or connivance of so bringing in or taking out such goods. 

 11. Section 25B of the SPA, closely read, suggests that anyone taking out of Bangladesh "any other goods" or bringing into Bangladesh "any goods" in breach of legal prohibition or restrictions or by evading payment of customs duties or taxes is liable to arrest on the charge of smuggling and susceptible to punishment by sentences ranging from death, imprisonment for life down to two years rigorous imprisonment as the Tribunal thinks proper in the peculiar facts of the case. There is no explanation of the phrase `any other goods' occurring in section 25B (1)(a) nor is there any explanation of the phrase "any goods" occurring in section 25B(1)(b). If the words 'any other goods' means all things that may be called 'goods' it naturally includes goods of every description. Therefore, it makes hardly any sense in mentioning in the section some goods specifically leaving others to be included within the phrase 'any other goods. The phrase "any goods" occurring in section 25B (1)(b) may fairly be construed to include each and everything that may be called goods. "Goods" in the Customs Act means 'all moveable goods' and includes conveyances, stores and materials, baggage, currency and negotiable instrument and electronic data. The crucial word 'goods' occurring in the Customs Act taken in isolation is apparently overbroad. But the law in which it appears being unilinear in scheme and intent the possibility of its abuse is limited by massive cognate words and phrases consistently qualifying it. But the SPA being a hybrid of several other legislations the phrases stand almost isolated from the context of law. Such overly broad and ambiguous phraseologies used in a penal clause of a stringent statute like the SPA has given absolute and unbridled power at the hands of the law enforcing agencies who now can haul up even a poor cultivator of a border-village coming across the border with half a kg salt and one kg onion for home consumption and easily put him behind the bar to be tried and punished for two years in prison, the lowest punishment prescribed under the law. 

 12. Here lies the crux of the SPA and fault-line between the original intention of the legislature behind the enactment of section 25B and the unguarded use of the heavier machineries of law to the suffering of the ordinary citizens never intended to suffer. It is an oft-quoted judicial dictum that parliament is presumed not to intend absurd or illogical result from the applications of its enactments. In the same vein it can fairly be said that parliament while enacting SPA had never foreseen a poor peasant or a couple of innocent students put behind the bar by applications of the law because the former came across the border with half kg salt and one kg onion and the latter came across the border with trifling things of their personal use having nothing to do with trade or business. Rather parliament in its anxiety tried to introduce heavier machineries of law in order to curve smuggling (as it is generally understood) adversely affecting national economy. It is a recognized principle of interpretation that where the purpose of an enactment is clear, it is often legitimate to put a strained interpretation upon some words which by its literal meaning defeats the purpose of the statute. In the words of Francis Bennion in Understanding Common Law Legislation: Drafting & Interpretation (First Indian reprint, 2004 p 43)-"The truth is that, sometimes arguments against a literal construction is so compelling that even though the words are not, within the rules of language, capable of another meaning they must be given one". The same spirit is resounded by our Supreme Court in SA Haroon vs Collector of Customs, 11 DLR (SC) 200, in the following words: "All rules of interpretation has been devised as aids to the discovery of the legislative intent behind an enactment. When the words are plain and unambiguous that intent can best be judged by giving full effect to the ordinary grammatical meaning of the words. But when this is not the case an attempt should be made to discover the true intent by considering the relevant provisions in the context of the whole Act in which it appears and by having regard to the circumstances in which the enactment came to be passed, the previous state of the law, the mischief sought to be suppressed and the new remedy provided are relevant factors to be given due considerations". 

 14. There are, however, 'goods' which are absolutely forbidden sometimes a small quantity or a single piece of which, if brought into Bangladesh, may constitute smuggling and the act of bringing in or possession thereof by persons not authorized so to do, may attract section 25B of the Special Powers Act, such as, fire arms, sculpture of antique value, narcotics and liquor, explosive substance and the like. In the cases of the kind the goods speak for itself and, as distinguished from other goods, self-evident as contraband. 

 15. Here in this juncture one thing cannot but be mentioned as a word of caution specially for courts and the tribunals trying cases of recovery of yaba tablets and puria of heroin. While trying the cases of the kind the courts/ tribunals must of necessity keep in mind that every case is likely to end in conviction and sentence passed on otherwise innocent men if they are oblivion of three things. First, generally in search and seizure express mandates of law and authorities are not followed and for want of experience most of the lawyers avoid cross-examination of the concerned officer on that point leaving the court/tribunal almost helpless. Second, in absence of any confrontation faced in court some of the police officers often find the so-called recovery of three puria of heroin or twenty two pieces yaba as a softer option to take into custody the person they want to put behind the bar. And it is not difficult for them with government uniform to stage a drama of recovery of heroin-puria or few pieces of yaba because before putting hands into the pocket of an innocent man they do not have to get themselves searched by any impartial member of the public, although law wants them to be so searched before pushing hands into someone's pocket or person. Third, rule of evidence has been currently relaxed allowing conviction to be sustained solely on the basis of evidence of some members of the raiding party and lastly, the absolute control of the I/O on the sample sent to the expert. Here lies the magic and the sample of the so-called recovered heroin/yaba may disappear and instead contents of the packet may be replaced by genuine yaba/ heroin. There is no authority to fruitfully oversee the unholy act done to the utter peril of the accused. 

 16. It is only the court/tribunal which remains to be the last hope for an innocent person. In these days of declining confidence in police investigation, stereo-type story of recovery and crisis of trial lawyers courts must rise to the rescue of innocent citizens and within their power insist on the strict observance of law and authority relating to search and seizure; strict proof of the story of recovery; credibility of the witnesses seeking to prove the recovery; possibility of victimization or of making a case with collateral purposes otherwise failing to hook up in specific cases and satisfaction of the court about the fact that actual sample of the madam recovered was sent to the expert which, if necessary, to be gathered by questioning the 1/0 on the point. And finally, painstaking scrutiny of the prosecution evidence against the defense line followed in cross-examination. 

 17. Reverting back to the point at hand, there is no scope for the phrases "any other goods" or "any goods" occurring in section 25B of the SPA to be taken in their plain literal meaning. Because, to do so is to make innocent millions vulnerable to the unbridled power of arrest and persecution by the law enforcing agencies and finally to bear the brunt of trial and punishment, as often is the case. Unnecessary sufferings unleashed to citizens by way of placing absurd construction on the phrase `any goods, not being the intention of the SPA, the phrases must be put not only to restrictive but also rectifying construction so as to ensure that the law is applied in keeping with its intent and thereby prevent agencies from proliferating misconceived smuggling cases to be tried at the cost of public time and money. 

 18. Here in this case the three young men were hauled up admittedly within the territory of Bangladesh possessed of trifling things of small value, such as, an ordinary wrist watch, a woolen sweater, few pieces underwear, a ball-pen, two cine-magazines, one jacket, a money bag, one packet cigarette and a small amount of Bangladeshi currency. Neither the BDR personnel nor the investigating officer did ever say that the seized goods were of commercial proportion so as to be reasonably called tradable merchandise. The nature, volume and value of the goods, that too of different types, are clearly suggestive of the fact that those are, brought, if at all, for personal use and far beyond the contemplation of section 25B of the SPA. None should be hauled up on the charge of smuggling merely because the goods were brought through unauthorized routes as it is well settled that all prohibited goods are not smuggled goods although all smuggled goods are prohibited goods. 

 For what we have said above, we find merit in this Rule. In the result, this Rule is made absolute. The impugned proceedings against the petitioners, namely, 1) Md Riad 2) Md Selim Haroon and 3) Md Shahjahan are quashed and they are discharged from the case and the sureties are released from the bail-bond. Order of stay earlier granted stands vacated.
